title: Reverse Linked List II
prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and two integers `left` and `right` (1-indexed), reverse the nodes of the list from position `left` to position `right`, and return the resulting list. Try to do it in a single pass.

The list is given as an array (e.g. `[1,2,3,4,5]` represents `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null`). The starter code includes helpers to convert between the array and a linked-list node — build the actual list, reverse the specified sublist by manipulating `next` pointers, then convert back to an array to return.
constraints: The number of nodes is n
hints: Use a dummy node before head so that a reversal starting exactly at the head doesn't need special-casing.
Walk to the node just before position `left` — call it `prev` — since that node's next pointer will need to point at the new front of the reversed section once you're done.

From `prev`, repeatedly take the node right after prev (always prev.next) and move it to the front of the sublist being reversed; doing this (right - left) times reverses the whole section in place in one pass.

solution.approach: Use a dummy node before head, and walk `prev` to the node immediately before position `left`. Then use the standard 'insertion at front' in-place reversal: repeatedly detach the node right after prev (which, after each iteration, is the next node still in its original position) and re-insert it right after prev, effectively pushing each subsequent node to the front of the reversed section one at a time. Doing this (right - left) times fully reverses the sublist in a single pass without needing extra space or a second traversal.
